Meeting Schedule

The regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month,

  1
 closed session business will usually commence at 5:30 p.m., when scheduled, and general business
session will commence at 6:30 p.m.

Brown Act

Agendas are drafted to accurately state what the legislative body is being asked to consider. The
legislative body can take action on "all items" listed on the agenda and be in compliance with the open
meeting laws. Under the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the
agenda, or unless certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The governing body may direct
staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for consideration at a future meeting.

City's Vision Statement

We envision a thriving, safe and inclusive community where everyone has the opportunity to access
exceptional services, education and support to be resilient and live full, vibrant lives.

Public Communications

Public Comments on agenda items are limited to three (3) minutes. All comments are to be addressed
directly to the Agency Members not to the members of the public.

Emails for public comment received prior to 4:00 pm on the day of the Council Meeting will be
summarized by the City Clerk, not read in its entirety. A copy of the email will be provided to the City
Council and will also be available at the City Clerk's Office for public review. A copy of each email will be
recorded for public record and noted on the official minutes of tonight's meeting.

Comments From The Audience - Non-Agenda Items
During this time, members of the public may address the City Council regarding any items not
listed on the agenda and within the subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council and not on
this agenda. Comments from the audience will be limited to three (3) minutes per speaker;
unless authorized by the Mayor, the time limit may not be extended by utilizing another
member's time. There will be no debate or action on items not listed on the agenda unless
authorized by law. The collective initial period of time for comments from the audience shall
be limited to 45 minutes. Any speaker that did not get a chance to speak during this segment

  3
 due to the 45-minute limitations will be able to speak at the end of the meeting prior to
adjournment.

Note: The City Council desires to provide all members of the public with the opportunity to
address the Council. Nevertheless, obscene language, comments intended to
disrupt/interfere, other actions which disrupt the progress of the meeting or slanderous
comments will not be tolerated and may result in ejection and/or may constitute a violation of
South Gate Municipal Code Section1.04.110.

Reports And Comments From City Officials
During this time, members of the City Council will report on matters pertaining to their service
on various intergovernmental boards and commissions as a representative of the City
pursuant to Assembly Bill 1234. City Council Members will also have an opportunity to
comment on matters not on the agenda.

Consent Calendar Items
Agenda Items 4 and 5 are Consent Calendar Items. All items including Ordinances,
Resolutions and Contracts, may be approved by adoption of the Consent Calendar,
individually and collectively by one (1) motion. There will be no separate discussion of these
items unless Members of the City Council, the public, or staff request that specific items be
removed from the Consent Calendar for separate discussion and action. Members of the
public are permitted to speak on any item listed but their time period is limited to three (3)
minutes in total.

Any motion to introduce or adopt an Ordinance on the Consent Calendar shall be: (1) a
motion to waive the reading of the Ordinance and introduce the Ordinance or (2) a motion to
waive the reading of the Ordinance and adopt the Ordinance, as appropriate.

GENERAL NOTICE TO THE PUBLIC

The City Council adopted new rules relating to the conduct of the public meetings, proceedings, and

  5
 business in the City of South Gate on July 12, 2022, (Resolution 2022-38-CC) and go into effect on
August 1, 2022. Resolution #2022-38-CC is available at the City Clerk’s Office.

MEETING SCHEDULE

Regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month, closed
session meetings will commence at 5:30 p.m. unless posted otherwise on its agenda. The regular City
Council meetings will commence at 6:30 p.m. Agendas are available at the following locations: City Clerk
Office, Public Notice Boards at City Hall, and on the City’s web page at https://www.cityofsouthgate.org

The Public can sign up to receive automatic notices of postings of agendas for the City Council or any
other Commission or Board of the City of South Gate. Visit the City webpage and click on the Agenda &
Minutes icon. That will take you the page where an individual can enter their email in the “Email
Updates” box to register.

PUBLIC COMMENT/PARTICIPATION

Any person may request to address a legislative body during a public meeting. The Presiding Officer will
call upon those present in the Council Chambers.

Speakers are limited to three (3) minutes on any item listed on the agenda, including public hearings.
Under Comments from the Audience portion, speakers are also limited to a single three (3) minutes time
limit. Comments from the Audience is initially limited to 45 minutes at each meeting. Any speaker still
wishing to speak, that did not speak, will have an addition Comments from the Audience opportunity after
the last business item is finished. The Presiding Officer may extend the time limit as long as there is no
objection from the City Council as a body.

To ensure that the public is able to participate, the City provides the opportunity to submit their
comments in person, email, mail. Methods of participation may be subject to change during other such
times when a State of Emergency, Health Order or State Executive Order limits in-person participation.

CURFEW

In absence of a motion duly adopted by majority vote of the City Council, the Presiding Officer may
adjourn the City Council meetings at 10:30 p.m. The Presiding Officer may ask the City Council if any
agenda items listed should be continued or dealt with during the meeting. For those items to be
continued, the City Council can direct the item be placed on the next City Council agenda or the current
meeting may be adjourned to a time certain at which time the meeting shall be reconvened as an
Adjourned Regular Meeting of the City Council and action upon the published agenda continued.

STAFF REPORTS

As a general rule, staff reports. or other written documentation are prepared/organized with respect to
each item of business listed on the agenda. Meeting agendas and staff reports are available at least 72-
hours prior to the scheduled regular City Council meeting and a minimum of 24-hours prior to a Special
City Council meeting. There are times when the City Council receives written material. revised material
after the posting of agendas, these materials are become a public record and will be available for public
view within 72-hours after the meeting in which they were received. Those materials and any other public
document can be inspected in the City Clerk's Office located at 8650 California Avenue, South Gate.

SERVICES TO FACILITATE ACCESS TO PUBLIC MEETINGS

In compliance with the American with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in the
City Council Meetings, please contact the Office of the City Clerk. Notification 48 hours prior to the City
Council Meeting will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to assure accessibility. For

  6
 further information, please contact the Office of the City Clerk at (323) 563-9510 or via email at
yglaze@sogate.org.

SUBJECT:  SUBST  ANTIAL  AMENDMENTS  TO  FISCAL  YEAR  2023-2024,  2024-2025,  &
2025-2026  ANNUAL  ACTION  PLANS  FOR  THE  COMMUNITY  DEVELOPMENT  BLOCK
GRANT  (CDBG)  FUNDS.

PURPOSE:  To consider  approving  Substantial  Amendments  to the FY 2023-2024  (No. 2), 2024-2025
(No. 2), & 2025-2026  (No. 1) Annual  Action  Plans to reprogram  CDBG  funds.

RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  Staff  recommend  that the City  Council  open the Public  Hearing,
receive  public  testimony,  and continue  the item  to the regularly  scheduled  City  Council  meeting  on
March  10, 2026

FISCAL  IMPACT:  There  is no fiscal  impact  to the City's  General  Fund.

NOTICING  REQUIREMENT:  Advertising  and notification  of the Public  Hearing  was conducted
in  compliance  with  Municipal  Code  Section  11.50.020  (Public  Hearing  Notification)  and  was

published  in The  South  Gate  Press  newspaper  on January  22,  2026.  The  notice  noted  a 30-day
comment  period.  Additionally,  the Notice  was posted  on the City's  website.

ALIGNMENT  WITH  COUNCIL  GOALS:  The FY 2025-2026  Annual  Action  Plans  supports  the
City  Council  goals  of creating  and protecting  strong  and sustainable  neighborhoods  by supporting
projects  and programs  that benefit  low-and  moderate-income  residents  of South  Gate.

ANALYSIS:  InaccordancewiththeCity'sCitizenParticipationP1an,whenprocessingasubstantial
amendment,  the City  is required  to hold  a 30-day  public  comment  period  and publish  a public  notice
speci:tying  the date, time,  and location  of a public  hearing.  Substantial  Amendment  No. 2 to the Fiscal
Year  2023-2024  Annual  Action  Plan  reduces  the  allocation  of  the  CDBG  2024  Neighborhood
Revitalization  Grant  Program  so that the funds  may be programmed  to the same program  but for the
current  fiscal  year.  Substantial  Amendment  No.  2 to the Fiscal  Year  2024-2025  Annual  Action  Plan
removes  three CDBG  South  Gate Park Improvement  projects  and adds additional  to one CDBG  South
Gate Park  Improvement  as noted  in the table  below.  Substantial  Amendment  No.  1 to Fiscal  Year
2025-2026  Annual  Action  Plan  removes  and reprogram  funds  allocated  to the CDBG  2025  Small
Business  Grant Assistance  Program,  increases  the allocation  of the 2025 Neighborhood  Revitalization
Grant  Program,  and programs  available  to a Demolition  & Clearance  project;  additionally  it reduces

CDBG:  Neighborhood  Revitalization  Grant  Program  - $60,000  proposed

The Neighborhood  Revitalization  Grant Program  provides  grants to income-eligible  households  for
eligible  home repairs.  The 2024 Neighborhood  Revitalization  Grant Program  assisted four households.
By reallocating  the balance  ($60,000)  to the 2025 Neighborhood  Revitalization  Grant Program,  the
program  will be able to assist additional  households,  with atotal updated proposed  budget of $425,000.

CDBG:  Parks  and Recreation  Improvements  - $64,254  proposed

Aquatics  Score Board  - $64,254 is proposed  to be added to this project,  for a total updated proposed
budget of $144,254.  The project  proposes to purchase  and install  a scoreboard  at the South Gate Park
Swim Stadium.

 CDBG:  Demolition  & Clearance  - $225,000  proposed

9001-9019  Long  Beach  Blvd  - $225,000  is proposed  for demolition  and clearance,  including  lead and
asbestos testing  and abatement,  of the South  Gate Housing  Authority  properties  located  at 9001-9019
Long  Beach  Blvd.

HOME:  Residential  Rehab  Program  - $340,000  proposed

Residential  Rehab  Program  - $340,000  is proposed  to be added to this residential  rehab program  to
assist additional  residents.

BACKGROUND:  The  City  of  South  Gate  has received  Community  Development  Block  Grant
(CDBG)  funds  annually  since  the enactment  of the Housing  and Cornrnunity  Development  Act  of
1974.  The City  qualifies  as an "entitlement"  jurisdiction  due to its population  exceeding  50,000  and
meeting  specific  demographic  criteria.  CDBG  funds  support  a variety  of projects  and programs  that
primarily  benefit  low-  and moderate-income  individuals.

Per HUD  regulations,  the development  ofAnnual  Action  Plans requires  citizen  participation  and public
review  process,  including  a public  hearing  before  submitting  any substantial  amendments.

The proposed  substantial  amendment  was presented  to the Citizens  Advisory  Committee  (CAC)  on
February  18, 2026, where  the CAC  reviewed  the proposal  and provided  funding  recornrnendations,  as
outlined  in the table above.

 SUBJECT:  REPORT  ON SOUTH  GATE'S  BUDGET  ST ATUS  AND  THE  COMPONENTS
 REQUIRED  TO  BE  COMPLETED  TO  DESIGN  A UTILITY  USERS  TAX  MEASURE
 INCLUDING  RESOLUTIONS  DECLARING  A FISCAL  EMERGENCY  AND  CALLING
 FOR  A SPECIAL  ELECTION  ON JUNE  2, 2026

 PURPOSE:  To educate  the Cornrnunity  and Council  on the current  state of the City's  budget
 and the structural  deficit  that currently  exists.  A description  of potential  budget  cuts to services
 will  be presented  and an outline  of how a Utility  Users Tax measure  is constructed  with  a sample
 version  will  be presented.  Resolutions  have been prepared  for discussion  and possible  adoption  for
 both  the Declaration  of a Fiscal  Emergency,  and to Call  a Special  Election  on Tuesday  June 2,
 2026, to adopt an Ordinance  for a Utility  Users Tax measure,  subject  to voter  approval.

 RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider:
  a.  Adopting  a Resolution  declaring  a Fiscal  Emergency;
  b.  Adopting  a Resolution  calling  a Special  Election,  request  that the Los Angeles  County
  Board  of  Supervisors  ("Board  of  Supervisors")  authorize  the  Los  Angeles  County
  Registrar-Recorder  / County  Clerk  ("County  Elections  Official")  to render  all  services
  necessary  to conduct  the Election,  allow  for Ballot  Arguments,  and an Impartial  Analysis;
  and
  c.  Reviewing  the draft Ordinance  for voter  consideration  of the Utility  Users Tax.

 FISCAL  IMPACT:  Election  expenses  are expected  to be approximately  $258,457  and were not
 included  in the current  fiscal  budget.  Election  costs will  be funded  from  available  General  Fund
 reserves.

 NOTICING  REQUIREMENTS:  None  required.

 ANALYSIS:  The City  has been able to sustain  a high  level  of community  services  and retain
 quality  City  staff and services  providers  by actively  pursuing  and recovering  "one-time"  revenues
 to fill  the City's  growing  structural  deficit.  During  this time,  revenues  within  the City's  General

  1

  19
 Fund,  sales tax,  property  tax,  and Vehicle  License  Fees remained  static  with  some  growth  in

property  tax, but  with  limited  or no growth  in the other  General  Fund  revenue  sources.  More
recently,  all Cities  are facing  a significant  downward  adjustment  to revenue  from the current  tariff
challenges  and the downward  trend  in the economy.  South  Gate, like  most  other  cities,  is being
significantly  impacted  by these trends.  The rising  costs for energy,  materials,  supplies  and services
along with  limited  growth  in revenue  have contributed  to the City's  structural  deficit,  which  is now
projected  to reach $9,000,000  for the coming  fiscal  year.

Recap  of Adopted  Budget
As reported  to the City  Council  on July  22, 2025,  the General  Fund  unassigned  balance  was
projected  to be $3,135,356  on July 1, 2025.  General  Fund revenues  are budgeted  at $70,943,552,
an amount  insufficient  to sustain  current  service  levels  without  reliance  on one-time  measures.
Expenditures  are budgeted  at $78,157,559  for fiscal year 2025-26,  resulting  in a structural  shortfall
of over $7 million.

Due to the exhaustion  of prior  one-time  federal  relief  fiu'ids;  legally  constrained  growth  in core
revenues  under Proposition  13; softening  and volatile  sales tax receipts;  declining  interest  earnings
resulting  from  reduced  fund  balances;  and substantial,  non-discretionary  increases  in pension
contributions,  insurance  premiums,  and  inflation-driven  operating  costs,  the  City's  ongoing
expenditure  materially  exceeds  its recurring  revenues.

As a result,  the City is experiencing  a structural  operating  deficit  exceeding  $7 million  in FY 2025-
26, which  is being temporarily  mitigated  through  the use of reserves  and interfund  transfers.  These
measures  are non-recurring  and unsustainable.  Based  on the City's  adopted  multi-year  financial
forecast,  the General  Fund deficit  is projected  to increase  to more than $9 million  in FY 2026-27,
at which  point remaining  discretionary  reserves  will  be insufficientto  support  continued  operations
at current  service  levels.

Absent  immediate  action,  the continued  depletion  of limited  General  Fund reserves  will  impair  the
City's  ability  to maintain  essential  public  safety,  infrastructure,  and community  services,  thereby
posing  a current  and  immediate  threat  to the  public  health,  safety,  and  welfare.  Delays  in

addressing  this  condition  would  result  in severe  budget  cuts that will  create  significant  cuts to
current  services  currently  offered  by the City.  If no additional  revenue  is funded  by the end of the
current  25/26  Fiscal  Year,  a $9,000,000  cut to City  services  will  be required.  This cut will  impact
on all general  fund  services  including  services  provided  by the Police,  Parks  and Recreation,
Community  Development,  and Public  Works  departments.

City's  Actions  to Close  the Budget  Deficit
The City  Council  and City  staff have not stood idly by knowing  that a fiscal  crisis was coming.  To
be fiscally  responsible,  the City  has done the following:
  *  Reorganized  and consolidated  Departments  to create more  efficiency.
  *  Increased  fees for general  services,  and increased  sewer rates to eliminate  the general  fund
  from  subsidizing  that service.
  *  Enacted  a personnel  hiring  freeze  for non-essential  functions  and services.
  *  Reviewed  staff salary allocations  to maximize  the use of water and special  funding  sources.
  *  Reviewed  City  operations  for operational  and cost efficiencies.

  2

  20
 City staff and City  Council  continue  to review  operations  and reduce  City costs; unfortunately,  the
scope and size of the General  Fund deficit  cannot  be solved  with  cost-cutting  measures  alone.

Potential  Revenue  Enhancement  Measure  to Protect  and Maintain  Vital  Services
The General  Fund  deficit  is approximately  9.2%  of the overall  General  Fund  budget,  even with
the reductions  noted  above.  To address  the $7.21  million  structural  deficit  will  require  a new
revenue  source.  Without  a strong  and reliable  revenue  source, the City will  not be able to maintain
and improve  City  services  such as police  anti-gang  and anti-drug  programs,  neighborhood  graffiti
abatement  programs,  after school  and park and recreation  programs,  and senior  services.

As proposed,  the voters  of the City  of South  Gate will  be asked to approve  a UUT.  The revenue
raised would,  legally,  be required  to be used in the City  of South Gate and could not be taken away
by the County  or the state. The revenue  collected  will  be sufficient  to eliminate  the structural  deficit
and to maintain  and improve  vital  City  services.  Without  new revenue,  the City  will  be forced  to
reduce  essential  community  services  beginning  in the next fiscal  year.

Required  Council  Actions
The City  Council  is being  presented  with  all the required  resolutions  for action.  The resolution
declaring  a fiscal  emergency  will  require  a unanimous  vote  of the City  Council.  The resolution
that calls for a special  municipal  election  approves  the ballot  question  with  a directive  for the City
Attorney  to prepare  an impartial  analysis  and provide  support  and opposition  arguments  and
rebuttals  for the Election  ballot  requires  a 4/5'h super majority  vote of the City  Council.

The legal deadline  to place a ballot  measure  on the June 2, 2026, election  ballot  is March  6, 2026.
A decision  now helps to ensure that all informational  materials  can be disseminated  to the voters
in a timely  fashion  and that there is ample  time for the request  and collection  of absentee  ballots.

BACKGROUND:
The City's  Current  Budget  Challenge
The City  is facing  a structural  budget  deficit,  meaning  the ongoing  cost of delivering  essential,
municipal  and utility  services  is higher  than the revenue  the City receives.  This deficit  is not a one-
time  issue; it is ongoing  and long-term  and will  continue  to grow  unless  action  is taken.  Without
new,  reliable  funding,  the City  will  eventually  be unable  to maintain  current  service  levels.

'Why  a Utility  Users  Tax  (UUT)?
A UUT  would  provide  a stable,  dedicated  general  fund revenue  source to provide  :funds to pay for
City services.  All  surrounding  south Los Angeles  cities have an active  Utility  Users Tax to provide
significant  general  fund revenue.  South  Gate has never had a Utility  Users Tax to provide  revenue
for general  fund services.

If a UUT  measure  was passed in South  Gate, the budget  deficit  would  be fixed,  and current  service
levels  would  be maintained.  This funding  would  help close the structural  gap and ensure the City
can maintain  police,  parks and recreation,  community  development,  and public  works  services  for
the community.

  3

  21
 Benefits  to Residents
A UUT  helps  the City  avoid  significant  service  reductions  in the future.  These  services  include
Police  911 response,  school  crossing  guards,  parks and recreation  facilities  and programs,  special
events,  plaru'iing,  building  and code enforcement  services,  and public  works  services.  The UUT
also supports  long-term  financial  stability  and responsible  management  of community  resources.

The Cost  of Doing  Nothing
Without  a new revenue  source,  the City  will  need to consider:
  *  Cutting  service  levels,  including  municipal  and infrastructure  services.  The presentation
  that will  be provided  outlines  the scope  of the projected  budget  cuts to service  and the
  impacts  these will  have on the community.
  *  Delaying  maintenance  or upgrades,  which  can increase  long-term  costs.
  *  Using  emergency  reserves,  however,  the City currently  has a minimum  amount  of reserves
  that meet industry  standards  for fiscal  health.  Drawing  down these reserves  any further  will
  not be sustainable  or fiscally  responsible.

The UUT  is a proactive  measure  that  allows  the City  to stabilize  its budget,  protect  essential
services,  and plan responsibly  for the future.  The UUT  also provides  a funding  stream  to preserve
vital  City  services.

  WHEREAS,  without  an immediate  source  of new  revenue,  the City  will  be forced  to
reduce  essential  services  to the community;

  WHEREAS,  maintaining  public  safety  with  a fully  funded  police  department,  continuing
to provide  school  crossing  guards,  maintairung  parks  and recreation  services,  senior  services,
neighborhood  graffiti  abatement  programs,  maintaining  responsive  planning,  building,  and code
enforcement  services,  and fixing  streets and potholes,  are essentials  for our community;
  WHEREAS,  without  the adoption  and submission  of a Utility  Users  Tax measure  to the
voters,  the City  will  be required  to implement  immediate  and significant  reductions  to existing
service  levels,  including  reductions  affecting  public  safety  operations,  parks  and  recreation
programming,  cornmuruty  development  services,  public  works  maintenance  activities,  financial
administration,  and the school  crossing  guard program,  due to the insufficiency  of ongoing  General
Fund revenues;
  WHEREAS,  a Utility  Users Tax measure  will  maim  it possible  for the City  to improve  its
overall  community  services,  for example  by: hiring  additional  police  officers  to reduce  emergency
response  times,  fixing  City  streets to improve  traffic  flow  and reduce  congestion,  fighting  gangs

Section  7.29.200  Remedies  Cumulative

All  remedies  and penalties  prescribed  by this  chapter  or which  are available  under  any other
provision  of law or equity  are cumulative.  The use of one or more  remedies  by the city  shall not
bar the use of any other remedy  for the purpose  of enforcing  the provisions  of tis  chapter  provided
only that the city may not collect  any liability  under this chapter  more than once.

Section  7.29.210  Notice  of Changes  to Ordinance

If a tax under  this chapter  is added,  repealed,  increased,  reduced,  or the tax base is changed,  the
tax  administrator  shall  provide  notice  as Public  Utilities  Code  Section  799  requires.  Before
effective  date of the ordinance  change,  each service  supplier  shall  provide  the tax administrator
with  a copy  of any written  procedures  describing  the information  the service  supplier  needs to
implement  the ordinance  change.  If the service  supplier  fails  to provide  such written  instructions,
the tax administrator,  or his or her agent,  shall  send, by first  class mail,  a copy  of the ordinance
change to all collectors  and remitters  of the city's  utility  users taxes according  to the latest payment
records  of the tax administrator.

Section  7.29.220  Future  Amendment  to Cited  Statute

Unless  specifically  provided  otherwise,  any reference  to a state or federal  statute  in this chapter
shall mean such statute  as it may be amended  from  time to time,  provided  that such reference  to a

  SUBJECT:  RESOLUTION  APPROVING  A  PERMANENT  EASEMENT  TO
  SOUTHERN  CALIFORNIA  EDISON  COMPANY  FOR  THE  CONSTRUCTION,  USE,
  OPERATION,  AND  MAINTENANCE  OF  OVERHEAD  AND  UNDERGROUND
  ELECTRICAL  FACILITIES  ON  CITY-OWNED  PROPERTY  AT  4035  TWEEDY
  BOULEVARD  (LELAND  R. WEAVER  LIBRARY)  TO  SERVE  VEHICLE  CHARGING
  STATIONS

  PURPOSE:  To  adopt  a Resolution  granting  a permanent  easement  to  Southern  California
  Edison  Company  (SCE)  on City-owned  property  at 4035  Tweedy  Boulevard,  the Los  Angeles
  County  Leland  R.  Weaver  Library,  to allow  the  installation,  operation,  and maintenance  of
  electrical  infrastructure  needed  to serve public  electric  vehicle  (EV)  charging  stations  as part of
  the Charge  Ready  Program.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider:
  a.  Adopting  a Resolution  granting  a permanent  easement  to the Southern  California  Edison
  Company  (SCE)  for the construction,  use, operation,  and maintenance  of electrical
  infrastnicture  at 4035 Tweedy  Boulevard  in support  of vehicle  charging  stations  serving
  the Los Angeles  County  Leland  R. Weaver  Library;  and
  b.  Authorizing  the  Mayor  to  execute  the  Easement  in  a form  acceptable  to  the  City
  Attorney.

  FISCAI,  IMPACT:  There  is no fiscal  impact.  The pernnanent  easement  will  be granted  to SCE
  at no cost and compensation  to the City.

  ANALYSIS:  State law allows  the City  to grant  easements  and similar  access rights  to regulated
  utility  companies,  as long  as the City  Council  approves  the terms.  This  authority  allows  the City
  to let utilities use City prope'm7 for essential services while keeping control over how that
  property  is used.

  SCE, a regulated  electric  utility,  is requesting  a permanent  easement  on City-owned  property  at
  4035  Tweedy  Boulevard,  the site of the Leland  R. Weaver  Library.  The easement  would  allow
  SCE to install  and maintain  electrical  equipment,  both  above  and below  ground,  needed to serve

  1

  97
 EV charging  stations  at this location.

The EV  charging  stations  are part of SCE's  Charge  Ready  Program,  which  helps  expand  access
to  EV  charging  infrastructure  in  the  community  and  supports  cleaner,  more  sustainable
transportation  options.

Granting  this  easement  allows  the electrical  infrastructure  to be installed  while  the City  keeps
full  ownership  of the property.  It also allows  SCE to operate  and maintain  the equipment  at its
own  cost, with  no financial  impact  to the City.  In addition,  the easement  supports  coordination
with  the Los Angeles  County  Library,  which  is participating  in the program,  ensuring  the EV
chargers  are installed  and operated  safely  and efficiently.

BACKGROUND:  The  Leland  R. Weaver  Library  is currently  undergoing  renovations  and is
scheduled  to reopen  in 2026.  As part  of planned  improvements  at the site, the library  is also
participating  in SCE's  Charge  Ready  Program,  which  provides  EV  charging  infrastnicture  at
public  facilities.

Under  the  Charge  Ready  Program,  SCE  will  install  the  required  electrical  infrastructure  to
support  EV  charging  stations  at the  library  at no cost  to the City.  The  EV  chargers  will  be
operated  in coordination  with  the Los Angeles  County  Library  and will  provide  public  access to
EV charging  while  supporting  cleaner  transportation  options.

Because  the  City  owns  the  property  where  the  electrical  infrastructure  will  be installed,  an
easement  is required  to allow  SCE to install,  operate,  and maintain  the equipment.  Approval  of
the easement  enables  the project  to move  forward,  preserves  City  ownership  of the property,  and
does not create any financial  obligation  for the City.

CITY OF SOUTH GATE
  REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  MINUTES
  TUESDAY, FEBRUARY 24, 2026

CALL TO ORDER  Joshua Barron, Mayor called a Regular City Council Meeting to order at
  6:30 p.m.

INVOCATION  Tina De La Rosa, Acting Director of Parks & Recreation
PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE  Jose De La Paz, City Treasurer

ROLL CALL  Yodit Glaze, City Clerk

PRESENT  Mayor Joshua Barron, Vice Mayor Al Rios, Council Member Maria del
  Pilar Avalos, Council Member Gil Hurtado, and Council Member Maria
  Davila; City Treasurer Jose De La Paz, City Manager Rob Houston, City
  Attorney Raúl F. Salinas

1
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING  The City Council opened the Public Hearing, received public testimony,
  and continued the item to the regularly scheduled City Council meeting on
  March 10, 2026, by motion of Council Member Hurtado and seconded by
  Council Member Avalos.
2
PROPERTY USE
ADMIN/PERMITS  The City Council opened the Public Hearing, received public testimony,
  and continued the item to the regularly scheduled City Council meeting on
  March 10, 2026, by motion of Council Member Hurtado and seconded by
  Council Member Avalos.

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Avalos, yes; v Council Member Hurtado,
  yes; Council Member Davila, yes; Vice Mayor Rios, yes; Mayor Barron,
  yes.
3
BUDGET ADMIN/
ELECTION ADMIN  The City Council considered:

  a. Adopting a Resolution declaring a Fiscal Emergency;

  b. Adopting a Resolution calling a Special Election, request that the Los
  Angeles County Board of Supervisors (“Board of Supervisors”)
  authorize the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk
  (“County Elections Official”) to render all services necessary to
  conduct the Election, allow for Ballot Arguments, and an Impartial
  Analysis; and
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF FEBRUARY 24, 2026
3
BUDGET ADMIN/
ELECTION ADMIN CONT’D
  c. Reviewing the draft Ordinance for voter consideration of the Utility
  Users Tax.

  Councilmember Davila thanked members of the public for their
  participation and input, both in support of and opposition to the proposed
  Utility Users Tax (UUT). She reiterated her position that the City
  Council’s responsibility is to declare a fiscal emergency and place the
  measure on the ballot, allowing voters to decide through the democratic
  process.

  She emphasized the importance of community education, noting concerns
  about misinformation, particularly on social media, and clarified that some
  sources are not affiliated with official City departments. Councilmember
  Davila stated that the decision to approve or reject the tax ultimately rests
  with the voters, not the Council, and reaffirmed her support for moving the
  measure forward to the ballot for public consideration.

  Councilmember Avalos acknowledged the presence of labor
  representatives and residents and thanked the public for their participation
  and input. She expressed concern regarding the City’s current fiscal
  deficit, noting prior awareness of financial challenges and emphasizing the
  need for accountability in past funding, including revenues generated
  through Measure P.

  Councilmember Avalos stated that now is not the appropriate time to
  increase taxes, citing the financial hardships faced by residents, including
  rising living costs, economic instability, and impacts to families, seniors,
  and vulnerable populations. She emphasized the importance of prioritizing
  the community’s financial well-being and avoiding additional burdens on
  residents.

  She called for greater transparency and accountability, including the
  potential establishment of an oversight body to monitor City revenues and
  expenditures, and raised concerns regarding the lack of ongoing reporting
  related to prior funding measures.

  Councilmember Avalos urged the City to explore alternative solutions to
  address the deficit, such as cost reductions, efficiency measures, and
  additional funding sources, before considering new taxes. She reaffirmed
  her commitment to representing and protecting the interests of residents,
  emphasizing trust, fiscal responsibility, and equitable solutions.
